1.heading: Handling Uncertainty & Ambiguity
1.idea: When there is no script, you can still take a first step. Learners practice breaking open-ended problems into "what I know, what I don't, what I can try."
1.tool: the Know / Don't Know / Try card. Three boxes learners fill in whenever a task feels unclear.
1.rep: Pick one unclear task this week. Fill the card before starting, then note what actually happened.

tiers.text: "Mystery Box" game: guess what's inside using clues, then say one thing they know and one thing they want to find out. Picture-based Try card.
A group project brief with deliberately vague requirements. Teams must write their own three success criteria before starting.
Open-ended case: "Your part-time job's manager quits mid-shift." Students map options and pick a first move with a reason.
Take a real ambiguous assignment or syllabus prompt. Write the Know / Don't Know / Try card, draft two questions for the professor, and submit one early draft.

sessions.title: No Instructions Included
sessions.hook: Hand out a task with missing directions (build a tower, plan an event) and watch what happens
sessions.rep: Fill the Know / Don't Know / Try card for the task, then attempt it

sessions.title: Good Questions Beat Guesses
sessions.hook: Show two people facing the same unclear task: one guesses, one asks
sessions.rep: Practice turning "I don't get it" into one specific question

sessions.title: Small Bets
sessions.hook: Story of an inventor or athlete who tested many small ideas
sessions.rep: Try three quick versions of a solution; keep the one that works best

sessions.title: Comfortable With Not Knowing
sessions.hook: Name the feeling: "stuck" is a signal, not a stop sign
sessions.rep: Group challenge that changes rules halfway through; debrief how they adapted

selfcheck: I can start a task even when directions are unclear
I know how to ask a good question

2.heading: Conflict Resolution & Compromise
2.idea: Disagreement is normal; how you handle it is a skill. Learners separate the problem from the person and look for the need underneath each position.
2.tool: the PAUSE method. Pause and breathe · Ask what happened from their side · Understand the need behind it · Share your side with an "I" statement · Explore options that meet both needs.
2.rep: Use PAUSE in one real disagreement. Note which step was hardest.
2.facilitator: This course practices everyday peer conflict. Situations involving bullying, harassment or safety go to a trusted adult or campus staff, and facilitators should say so in Session 1.

tiers.text: Puppet or picture-card role-plays about sharing, taking turns and being left out. "Peace Path" floor mat walked step by step.
Group-chat and lunch-table scenarios, including online misunderstandings. Practice a respectful "can we talk?" opener.
Team-project free-rider, sibling curfew fight, sports playing-time dispute. Students negotiate a written compromise.
Roommate agreement lab: pairs draft a shared-living agreement (noise, guests, cleaning). Plus a workplace scenario with a coworker who missed their part.

sessions.title: Same Story, Two Sides
sessions.hook: Retell a short conflict from each person's view
sessions.rep: Rewrite a blame sentence ("You always…") as an "I" statement

sessions.title: Listen to Understand
sessions.hook: Game of telephone shows how messages get twisted
sessions.rep: Partner listening: repeat back what you heard before replying

sessions.title: Needs, Not Positions
sessions.hook: Two kids want the same orange: one wants juice, one wants the peel
sessions.rep: Identify the need behind three common arguments

sessions.title: Find the Middle
sessions.hook: Show a win-lose, a lose-lose and a win-win ending
sessions.rep: Role-play a conflict start to finish using PAUSE

selfcheck: I can listen to someone I disagree with
I can find a compromise

3.heading: Absorbing & Applying Feedback
3.idea: Feedback is about the work, not your worth. Learners practice hearing it, sorting it and using it.
3.tool: Hear it, Sort it, Use it. Hear it without defending. Sort each comment into "use now," "ask about" or "set aside." Use one piece right away.
3.rep: Ask someone for feedback on one thing you made this week. Use one comment and log the result.

tiers.text: "Two Stars and a Wish" drawing critique. Kids practice saying "thank you" and trying the wish on a second drawing.
Peer review of a short paragraph or poster with sentence starters ("One thing that worked…" / "One thing to try…").
Essay or lab report with teacher-style comments; students write a revision plan. Add a mock job-interview debrief.
Bring a real graded paper or supervisor note. Draft a professional reply email and a three-step revision plan. Practice asking a professor for feedback in office hours.

sessions.title: Work ≠ Worth
sessions.hook: Coach's-eye clip or story: an athlete gets corrected and improves
sessions.rep: Write "The feedback is about ___, not about me" for three sample comments

sessions.title: The Sting Is Normal
sessions.hook: Name the body's reaction to criticism (hot face, urge to argue)
sessions.rep: Receive practice feedback and respond only with "Thanks, tell me more"

sessions.title: Sort the Pile
sessions.hook: A stack of mixed feedback on one project: helpful, vague, unkind
sessions.rep: Sort each comment into Use / Ask / Set Aside

sessions.title: Revise and Resubmit
sessions.hook: Show a first draft and its improved version side by side
sessions.rep: Revise one piece of their own work using one comment; share the before and after

selfcheck: I can hear criticism without getting defensive
I use feedback to improve

4.heading: Time Management & Prioritizing
4.idea: You can't do everything, so choose on purpose. Learners sort tasks by importance, protect focus time and plan around their real energy.
4.tool: the Big Rocks priority sort (Must / Should / Could), and the Energy Ledger, a daily check of school load, social load and physical tiredness before planning.
4.rep: Run one week with a Big Rocks list each morning. Count how many Musts got done.

tiers.text: Picture schedule and "first-then" boards. Sand-timer races to feel how long 5 minutes is.
Paper planner setup, homework-before-screens routine, and a 10-minute focus sprint.
Balance school, a job, sports and family. Build a weekly plan with the Energy Ledger; 20-minute focus sprints.
Syllabus-to-semester map: every deadline from every class on one calendar. Build a weekly schedule with class, work, study blocks and rest. 25-minute focus sprints.

sessions.title: Big Rocks First
sessions.hook: Jar demo: rocks, pebbles, sand; order changes what fits
sessions.rep: Sort a week of real tasks into Must / Should / Could

sessions.title: Where Did the Time Go?
sessions.hook: Guess vs. actual: how long do common tasks really take?
sessions.rep: Time-log one afternoon; compare guesses to reality

sessions.title: The Phone Problem
sessions.hook: Count notifications during a 10-minute task
sessions.rep: Try a phone-away focus sprint (10–25 min by tier) and compare output

sessions.title: Plan Backward
sessions.hook: Show a project due in two weeks and the panic the night before
sessions.rep: Break one assignment into dated steps on a calendar

selfcheck: I know what matters most this week
I can focus without my phone

5.heading: Self-Direction & Initiative
5.idea: Nobody is going to tell you every step, and that's your chance. Learners set their own goals, start without being told and hold themselves accountable.
5.tool: the Own-It Loop. Choose a goal · Set the first step · Start before you feel ready · Check in with yourself · Adjust.
5.rep: Start one thing this week before anyone reminds you. Log when you started and what happened.

tiers.text: Classroom "helper who notices" game: spot something that needs doing and do it without being asked. Sticker chart for self-started jobs.
Choose-your-own mini project (two weeks) with a self-made checklist and check-in dates.
Personal passion project or job/college application plan with milestones they set and track themselves.
"No one is taking attendance" lab: design a personal semester system (study hours, office hours visits, campus resources). Pair up as accountability partners with weekly check-ins.

sessions.title: Waiting vs. Starting
sessions.hook: Two students, same assignment: one waits for reminders, one starts
sessions.rep: List three things they usually wait to be told to do

sessions.title: My Why
sessions.hook: Short story of someone driven by a personal reason
sessions.rep: Write a personal "why" for one goal

sessions.title: The 2-Minute Start
sessions.hook: Show how starting is the hardest part
sessions.rep: Pick a stalled task and do only the first 2 minutes

sessions.title: Be Your Own Coach
sessions.hook: Compare a coach checking in vs. no one checking
sessions.rep: Set up a self-check-in routine and an accountability buddy

selfcheck: I start things without reminders
I check my own progress

6.heading: Resilience & Perseverance
6.idea: A setback is data, not a verdict. Learners practice the bounce-back cycle so a bad grade or failed try becomes the next attempt, not the end.
6.tool: the Reset Rep. Feel it (name the emotion) · Face it (what actually happened?) · Fix one thing · Try again.
6.rep: Next time something goes wrong, run the Reset Rep and log your second attempt.
6.facilitator: Some students carry heavier setbacks than a bad grade. Share school counselor or campus counseling contacts in Session 1, and refer anyone who seems in distress.

tiers.text: "Yet" power word ("I can't do it… yet"). Block-tower or balloon-balance game with multiple tries.
Low-stakes "Friction Reps": short speaking-in-front-of-group turns and tough puzzles, getting a bit harder each round.
Post-test recovery plan after a real bad grade, plus a college/job rejection role-play and response.
First-semester setback plan: midterm recovery, when to visit tutoring or the professor, withdrawal vs. push-through decision, and campus support resources.

sessions.title: Everyone Misses
sessions.hook: Famous failures: rejected authors, cut athletes, failed first products
sessions.rep: Share (or write privately) one time they failed and what came after

sessions.title: Name It to Tame It
sessions.hook: How stress feels in the body; box breathing
sessions.rep: Practice a 60-second reset: breathe, name the feeling, one next step

sessions.title: Autopsy, Not Attack
sessions.hook: Compare "I'm bad at math" with "I missed questions 4–7 because…"
sessions.rep: Analyze a sample failed test: what went wrong and one fix

sessions.title: Attempt Two
sessions.hook: Show improvement from attempt one to attempt three
sessions.rep: Deliberately hard challenge (puzzle, skill drill); log each attempt and what changed

selfcheck: After a setback I try again
I know how to calm down when upset

7.heading: Critical Thinking & Problem-Solving
7.idea: Knowing facts is step one; using them on a messy real problem is the goal. Learners practice defining problems, checking claims and testing solutions.
7.tool: the IDEAL steps. Identify the problem · Define what "solved" looks like · Explore options and evidence · Act on the best one · Look back and learn.
7.rep: Pick one real problem you face. Work it through IDEAL on paper and try your solution.

tiers.text: "Detective" mysteries with clues; sort facts from guesses. Fix-it challenges (a toy bridge that keeps falling).
Spot the misleading ad or post. Plan a class fundraiser using percentages and a budget.
Community problem project (school lunch waste, park safety) with evidence gathering and a proposal to a real decision-maker.
Case-study teams on a real campus or local issue. Written recommendation memo with evidence and trade-offs, presented to peers.

sessions.title: What's the Real Problem?
sessions.hook: "The bus is always late": is that the problem or a symptom?
sessions.rep: Ask "why?" five times on a real school or campus problem

sessions.title: Check the Claim
sessions.hook: Two headlines or posts about the same event that disagree
sessions.rep: Evaluate a claim: who says it, what's the evidence, what's missing

sessions.title: Use What You Know
sessions.hook: A classroom fact (fractions, percentages, a science idea) applied to a real task
sessions.rep: Solve a real-world problem with a school concept (budget a party, plan a garden)

sessions.title: Solve It Together
sessions.hook: Community challenge brief
sessions.rep: Teams work through IDEAL and pitch a solution in 2 minutes

selfcheck: I check whether claims are true
I can use what I learn on real problems

8.heading: SAT Prep (College Readiness)
8.idea: The SAT rewards calm pacing and fixing repeat mistakes more than cramming. This course applies the skills from the other Ava's Place courses to one high-stakes test on the road to college.
8.tool: the Error Log. For every missed question: topic · why I missed it (didn't know, misread, rushed, ran out of time) · the fix · retest date.
8.who: Launchers (grades 10–12) heading to college, plus adults re-entering school who need a score. Self-paced: 6 modules (short video, practice set, Error Log entry), about 60–90 minutes each. Learners move at their own speed, with a suggested pace of one module per week and an optional live Q&A office hour.
8.test: Fully digital in the Bluebook app. Two sections, Reading and Writing (64 min) then Math (70 min), each split into two adaptive modules. 98 questions, 2 hours 14 minutes of testing, 10-minute break, scored 400–1600. The Desmos calculator is available on all Math questions. (source, source)
8.rep: Register for a test date (or pick a target date) and complete two weeks of the study plan.
8.measure: Diagnostic score vs. final practice score, plus the drop in repeat errors in the Error Log.
8.free: official full-length practice tests in Bluebook and College Board's free Official Digital SAT Prep on Khan Academy. Families pay nothing extra.

sessions.title: Know the Test
sessions.hook: Walk through Bluebook: modules, tools, timing, how adaptive works
sessions.rep: Take a timed diagnostic module; start the Error Log

sessions.title: Reading & Writing Strategy
sessions.hook: One short passage, one question: read the question first
sessions.rep: Timed R&W practice set; log misses by type

sessions.title: Math Strategy + Desmos
sessions.hook: Solve one problem by hand and with Desmos, compare speed
sessions.rep: Timed Math practice set using Desmos where it saves time

sessions.title: Pacing Per Module
sessions.hook: Module 1 performance shapes Module 2, so don't rush the easy ones
sessions.rep: Pacing drill: flag, skip, return; two timed modules

sessions.title: Test-Day Nerves
sessions.hook: Link to Course 6 Reset Rep: breathing and the 60-second reset
sessions.rep: Full practice test under real conditions

sessions.title: Personal Study Plan
sessions.hook: Review the Error Log: which 3 mistake types cost the most?
sessions.rep: Build a 6–8 week plan with weekly timed modules and review sessions

selfcheck: I know how the digital SAT works
I have a study plan I can follow

9.heading: Entrepreneurship (College)
9.idea: Entrepreneurship is the other seven skills under real pressure. Students take a small idea from problem to first paying customer in six weeks, using uncertainty, feedback, resilience and problem-solving as working tools.
9.tool: the Build–Test–Learn Board. One page per week: what we believe · what we tested · what customers said or did · what we'll change.
9.who: Leaders (college and first-year adults). Self-paced: 6 modules (short video, worksheet, field task), with a suggested pace of one module per week. Progress is posted to an online Build–Test–Learn Board that a mentor reviews.
9.rep: Make one real sale, sign-up or pre-order, and log what it took.
9.measure: Customer interviews completed, tests run, and whether the team reached a first customer. Panel scores from Pitch Day.
9.options: campus service (tutoring, moving help), digital product, student-made goods, or a social-impact venture that benefits a nonprofit.

sessions.title: Problems Worth Solving
sessions.hook: Founder story that started with a personal frustration
sessions.rep: List 10 problems you or classmates face; pick one

sessions.title: Talk to Customers
sessions.hook: Show a product nobody wanted because no one asked
sessions.rep: Interview 5 potential customers with open questions; no pitching

sessions.title: The Smallest Test
sessions.hook: Examples of tests done in a weekend: a sign-up page, a pre-order, a pop-up
sessions.rep: Design a minimum viable test for under $50

sessions.title: Money Basics
sessions.hook: What a product costs vs. what it sells for
sessions.rep: Simple unit economics: price, cost, margin, break-even

sessions.title: Pivot or Persist
sessions.hook: Famous pivots where the first idea failed
sessions.rep: Review test results; decide to keep, change or drop the idea

sessions.title: Pitch Day
sessions.hook: 90-second pitch model: problem, customer, proof, ask
sessions.rep: Record a 90-second pitch video and submit it; a panel of local founders or alumni reviews it and sends written feedback

selfcheck: I can test an idea with real customers
I can pitch an idea with confidence

10.heading: Confidence & Self-Worth
10.idea: Confidence is built through reps, not born. Learners separate who they are from grades, likes and wins, and grow confidence through small, repeated acts of courage.
10.tool: the Evidence File. A running list of proof: things I tried, things I did even though I was nervous, times I kept going. When the inner critic talks, learners read their evidence.
10.rep: Complete 3 brave reps this week and add each one to your Evidence File.

tiers.text: "I Can" jar filled with notes of things they've learned to do. Show-and-tell with a strong voice and eye contact.
Social media comparison check: what's real vs. edited. Build an Evidence File and a personal "confidence playlist" of reminders.
Identity map (values, strengths, interests) separate from sports stats, GPA or followers. Practice a mock interview introduction.
Imposter-feeling lab for first-gen and new students: name it, gather evidence, speak in class or office hours once this week. Draft a personal introduction for networking and interviews.

sessions.title: I Am More Than a Score
sessions.hook: Two students with the same grade: one says "I'm dumb," one says "I need a new plan"
sessions.rep: Write 5 "I am…" statements that have nothing to do with grades, looks or wins

sessions.title: The Inner Critic
sessions.hook: Read an unkind inner voice out loud: would you say this to a friend?
sessions.rep: Rewrite 3 harsh self-talk lines as a coach would say them

sessions.title: Brave Reps
sessions.hook: Confidence comes after action, not before
sessions.rep: Pick a small brave act (ask a question, say hi, raise a hand) and do it this week

sessions.title: Speak Up
sessions.hook: Body language changes how you feel and how others hear you
sessions.rep: Give a 30-second to 2-minute talk (by tier) on something you care about

selfcheck: I like who I am even when I lose or fail
I can speak up in a group

11.heading: Peer Pressure & Independent Choices
11.idea: Fitting in shouldn't cost you who you are. Learners spot pressure (in person and online), practice saying no without losing face, and make choices they can own.
11.tool: the STOP check. Spot the pressure · Think ahead: what happens next? · Options: name at least two · Pick and own it.
11.rep: Use STOP once this week when you feel pressure, big or small. Log what you chose and why.
11.facilitator: Situations involving substances, safety or someone being hurt should go to a trusted adult or campus staff. Say this in Session 1 and share contacts.

tiers.text: Puppet scenes about copying, leaving someone out, and dares on the playground. Practice a strong "No thanks" voice and finding a grown-up.
Group-chat pressure, online challenges and trends, sharing photos, cheating on homework. Build a personal "exit line" and a code word with a parent.
Parties, driving, vaping, academic dishonesty and social media. Plan ahead for 3 real situations they expect this year.

New-environment pressure: going along with roommates, spending to keep up, skipping class, drinking culture, group-project shortcuts. Write a personal values list and one boundary to hold this semester.

sessions.title: Spot the Pressure
sessions.hook: Direct pressure ("Just do it") vs. quiet pressure (everyone else is doing it) vs. online pressure (dares, trends, group chats)
sessions.rep: Sort 10 scenarios by type of pressure

sessions.title: The Cool No
sessions.hook: Show a no that sounds awkward and one that sounds easy
sessions.rep: Practice 5 ways to say no: joke, excuse, switch the plan, walk away, straight no

sessions.title: Your Crew
sessions.hook: Friends who lift you vs. friends who push you
sessions.rep: Map your circle: who makes good choices easier, who makes them harder

sessions.title: Stand on Your Own
sessions.hook: Story of someone who went against the group and was glad later
sessions.rep: Role-play a group scenario using STOP, then debrief how it felt

selfcheck: I can say no to friends when something feels wrong
My choices reflect my own values

12.heading: Online Safety & Scam Smarts
12.idea: Scammers count on panic and shame. Learners practice slowing down, spotting the red flags and knowing exactly what to do and who to tell, so a bad moment online never turns into a crisis.
12.tool: the 3 Rs. Recognize the red flags (rush, secrecy, requests for money or photos, too good to be true) · Refuse to send, pay or click · Report it to a trusted adult and the platform, and save the evidence.
12.rep: Do a privacy and settings checkup on two apps you use, and share your safety plan with one trusted adult.
12.facilitator: Talk about sextortion calmly and without blame: the person targeted is never at fault. Share counselor contacts in Session 1 and know your school's reporting process; if a student discloses, follow your mandated-reporter procedures. Free help for young people: NCMEC's Take It Down (takeitdown.ncmec.org) helps remove explicit images, and the CyberTipline (report.cybertip.org) takes reports.

tiers.text: "Tricky people online" picture cards. Never share your name, school or photos, and always tell a grown-up. You will never be in trouble for telling.
Game chats, free-currency and giveaway scams, and friend requests from strangers. Do a privacy-settings check together.
Sextortion warning signs, fake jobs and money-flip scams, and text and QR-code scams. Walk through Take It Down and how to report.
Rental and housing scams, fake job offers with upfront fees, payment-app scams, and protecting your credit and identity.

sessions.title: Too Good to Be True
sessions.hook: Three messages: a prize, a job offer, a cheap deal. Which ones are real?
sessions.rep: Sort ten realistic messages into safe, suspicious or scam, and name the red flag in each

sessions.title: Who's Really There?
sessions.hook: A friendly new follower who already knows a lot about you
sessions.rep: Check a profile together: account age, mutual friends, reused photos (older tiers try a reverse image search)

sessions.title: Never Pay, Never Panic
sessions.hook: How threat scams use panic and shame to rush you (age-appropriate)
sessions.rep: Role-play the first ten minutes: stop replying, don't pay, screenshot, block, tell an adult, and report

sessions.title: Your Safety Team
sessions.hook: Who would you tell? Many young people say no one
sessions.rep: Build a no-shame family safety plan: a settings checkup, a code word, and three adults you can go to

selfcheck: I can spot the red flags of a scam
I know exactly what to do and who to tell if someone threatens me online

13.heading: NIL & Recruiting
13.idea: Your name, image and likeness can open doors, or close them if you sign the wrong thing. Athletes and their families learn the rules, the money and the red flags before the first offer arrives.
13.tool: the Deal Check. Before any deal: Is it allowed under my state and school rules? · What do I give and what do I get? · How and when am I paid, and what will I owe in taxes? · Who reviewed it: a parent, a coach, a qualified professional?
13.who: Launchers (grades 9–12) and college athletes, with a parent and guardian track. Self-paced: 6 modules (short video, worksheet, family discussion), with a suggested pace of one module per week.
13.parents: Parents and guardians often manage an athlete's first deals. The parent track covers the same Deal Check, how to vet agents and marketing reps, and keeping NIL money and records organized from day one.
13.measure: Deal Checks completed, brand statements written and pitches recorded.
13.rep: Run one real or sample offer through the Deal Check with a parent or mentor before saying yes.
13.facilitator: NIL rules differ by state and change often. Point high school families to their state athletic association and college athletes to their compliance office. This course is education, not legal or tax advice; encourage families to have any real contract reviewed by a qualified professional.

sessions.title: Know Your Rules
sessions.hook: The same deal in two states: allowed in one, an eligibility problem in the other
sessions.rep: Find your state association's NIL policy and list three rules that apply to you

sessions.title: Your Brand, Your Story
sessions.hook: Two athlete profiles: one sponsors want, one they avoid
sessions.rep: Audit your social media and write a two-sentence brand statement

sessions.title: Reading the Deal
sessions.hook: A sample agreement with three hidden traps
sessions.rep: Mark up a sample NIL agreement: exclusivity, length, deliverables and payment

sessions.title: Money & Taxes
sessions.hook: Why a $1,000 deal isn't $1,000 in your pocket
sessions.rep: Pick a set-aside percentage for taxes, start a simple income tracker, and learn what a 1099 form is

sessions.title: Recruiting & NIL Together
sessions.hook: How deals and social media can help or hurt recruiting
sessions.rep: Build a recruiting plan: highlight film, a coach contact list, a timeline and the questions to ask about NIL

sessions.hook: A 30-second pitch to a local business
sessions.rep: Record a pitch to a local business and get feedback from a parent or mentor

14.heading: Real Life Money
14.idea: Money gets real fast: a first paycheck, a first credit card, a first doctor's bill. Learners practice the money skills recent grads say they most wish they'd been taught.
14.tool: the Money Map. One page that shows what comes in (your pay stub) · what goes out (needs, wants, savings) · what you owe (credit and loans) · what protects you (insurance and an emergency fund).
14.rep: Build your own Money Map for a real or sample month, and share one money goal with a family member.
14.facilitator: Use sample documents, never students' real financial information. Tax rules and dollar thresholds change every year, so check IRS.gov for current figures. This course pairs well with the personal finance course many states now require.

tiers.text: Needs vs. wants, a three-jar save/spend/share game, and why grown-ups pay for things like the doctor.
First earnings from babysitting or mowing, a simple budget, and how a debit card differs from a credit card.
A first paycheck and W-4, a first tax return, credit basics before a first card, and staying on a family health plan.
Filing on your own, student loans and credit cards, choosing a health or student plan, and the costs of renting a first place.
